articles.title: ProRail awards Rotterdam rail yard upgrade contract to VolkerRail
articles.summary: ProRail has awarded VolkerRail a contract to redevelop the Waalhaven Zuid rail yard at the Port of Rotterdam, increasing its capacity to handle longer freight trains. articles.body: ProRail has awarded VolkerRail a contract to redevelop the Waalhaven Zuid rail yard at the Port of Rotterdam, increasing its capacity to handle longer freight trains. The contract was signed on October 15, 2026. Construction is scheduled to begin in late 2026 and continue until the end of 2028. The project will improve rail freight operations at the port, supporting growing demand for cargo transport between Rotterdam and inland destinations. Rail yard to accommodate 740-metre container trains The redevelopment will provide six tracks capable of handling freight and container trains up to 740 metres long. It will also add 12 locomotive parking spaces and upgrade the existing railway infrastructure, including further electrification. ProRail plans to improve the separation of secured and unsecured areas. This will allow train movements and shunting operations to take place more safely and efficiently. The project is expected to increase capacity at Waalhaven Zuid and improve its ability to handle growing freight volumes. Freight operations to continue during construction One of the main challenges is completing the redevelopment while keeping rail freight services running wherever possible. Space at the rail yard is limited, and the project must meet technical, environmental and permitting requirements. To address these challenges, ProRail has reached agreements with the Municipality of Rotterdam and the Port of Rotterdam Authority to secure temporary working space near the site. ProRail and VolkerRail will now finalise the construction arrangements. Rail operators, shippers and other stakeholders will receive updates on the works and any expected disruption. The project also receives financial support from the European Commission. According to ProRail, the investment will help Waalhaven Zuid meet increasing demand for rail freight services to and from the Port of Rotterdam.

articles.title: UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape
articles.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard. In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January...
articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Regulatory UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 0 1 minute read UK Government UK Government The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard. In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January 2025, had imposed a substantially greater administrative workload on shipowners and regulators than initially anticipated. The 22-page report identifies difficulties with reporting deadlines, fuel certification, emissions calculations and compliance pooling arrangements. Some operators missed deadlines despite meeting their operational obligations, while inconsistencies between verification systems created additional work. The Chamber wants the UK government to establish a fully tested ship-level monitoring and reporting system before introducing compliance obligations. It is also pushing for fuel-neutral regulation, realistic emissions targets based on fuel availability and infrastructure readiness, and flexibility for owners and operators to meet their obligations without unnecessary commercial disruption. Peter Aylott, the Chamber’s director of policy, said the government had an opportunity to learn from the EU’s experience rather than create another regulatory system that increased costs and complexity. The paper also calls for close alignment with emerging International Maritime Organization requirements to avoid duplicate certification, reporting and verification obligations. The intervention comes as the Department for Transport prepares to consult on a domestic maritime fuel standard, with the consultation expected later this year. Britain’s maritime decarbonisation strategy, unveiled in March 2025, targets a 30% reduction in domestic shipping’s lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, rising to 80% by 2040 and zero by 2050, against a 2008 baseline. The government has identified fuel regulation and emissions pricing as central measures for meeting those targets. articles.body: Europe Finance and Insurance Tankers Marinakis tanker venture locks down $930m for 11 VLCC newbuilds Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 42 1 minute read Capital Group Capital Group Greek shipowner Capital Tankers has lined up $930.3m in financing for 11 VLCC newbuildings under construction in China and South Korea, making further headway in funding its expanding crude tanker fleet. The Evangelos Marinakis-backed company has signed four financing arrangements since late September, covering vessels booked at Hanwha Ocean, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Co (DSIC) and Hengli Shipbuilding. The largest portion, totalling $450.6m, covers five 307,000 dwt VLCCs at DSIC. Three vessels are being financed at between $89.6m and $90.9m each under an October agreement, with another two securing $89.6m apiece. Capital Tankers has also arranged $241.8m for three 320,000 dwt LNG dual-fuel-ready VLCCs at South Korea’s Hanwha Ocean, alongside $237.9m for three 306,000 dwt vessels at Hengli in China. The Hanwha financing carries a five-year repayment schedule, while the Chinese yard packages are structured over ten years. All include substantial balloon payments at maturity, ranging from $39.7m to $60.9m per vessel. The company has not identified the financing providers. Separately, Capital Tankers has disclosed a $64.5m sale-and-leaseback arrangement for its newly delivered 155,348 dwt LNG dual-fuel suezmax Amor , built at New Times Shipbuilding in China. The financing, arranged earlier this year, runs to October 2033, with a $40m final payment. The latest financing commitments follow Capital Tankers’ $500m Oslo private placement earlier this year, which was upsized after strong investor demand as the Marinakis group brought its crude tanker business to the public market. The owner has since continued adding tonnage. In June, it acquired three VLCC newbuilding contracts at Hengli from parent Capital Maritime & Trading at $122m apiece, with deliveries scheduled for the second half of 2027. Capital Tankers now controls a 33-vessel fleet comprising 15 VLCCs, 10 suezmaxes and eight aframax/LR2 tankers. Seventeen vessels are trading, with another 16 due for delivery through mid-2028. The company also retains options for 13 additional crude tankers. articles.body: Containers Europe Euroseas seals bumper charter and $26m boxship sale Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 43 1 minute read Euroseas Euroseas Nasdaq-listed Greek containership owner Euroseas has secured a $62,500-a-day charter for a 25-year-old feeder vessel while agreeing to sell its sistership for $26m, capitalising on continued strength in the smaller boxship market. The Aristides Pittas-led company said its 2001-built, 2,556 teu EM Corfu has been fixed for a minimum of 12 and maximum of 14 months at the charterer’s option. The new contract will begin in mid-December, following a scheduled drydocking, and represents a sharp increase from the vessel’s previous employment at $28,000 per day. Euroseas expects the minimum charter period to generate approximately $17.8m in EBITDA. The company has also agreed to sell the 2001-built, 2,556 teu Evridiki G to an unrelated third party for approximately $26m. The vessel is expected to change hands at the end of October, once its current charter expires. Euroseas anticipates recording an accounting gain of approximately $22.5m from the disposal. Both vessels were previously fixed in November 2024, with EM Corfu securing $28,000 per day and Evridiki G $29,500 per day. The latest charter more than doubles EM Corfu’s previous daily rate, while the sale allows Euroseas to realise a substantial gain from its sistership without undertaking another costly drydocking. Following the disposal, Euroseas will operate 20 containerships with a combined capacity of approximately 58,600 teu. The company also has 12 vessels under construction in China, ranging from 1,800 teu feeders to 4,484 teu intermediate containerships, with deliveries scheduled between 2027 and 2029. articles.summary: Dutch inland shipping companies Amer Shipping and Van de Graaf & Meeusen have joined forces to establish a new chartering business in Antwerp, backed by a fresh dry cargo newbuilding order at Concordia Damen. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Operations Dutch inland shipping duo expands into Belgium with new chartering venture Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 36 1 minute read TriBarge TriBarge Dutch inland shipping companies Amer Shipping and Van de Graaf & Meeusen have joined forces to establish a new chartering business in Antwerp, backed by a fresh dry cargo newbuilding order at Concordia Damen. The two family-owned operators have launched TriBarge to target Belgian and French shippers, combining their existing networks and vessel capacity with plans for joint fleet investment. The new company will handle dry cargo, general cargo and breakbulk movements across the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region, German canals, the Moselle and inland waterways reaching Basel. Through its partnership with Stream Shipping, an existing venture between Amer Shipping and German cooperative MSG eG, TriBarge will also be able to serve destinations as far as the Black Sea. The partners have already contracted an 85 m dry cargo vessel at Concordia Damen. The newbuilding, to be named Porta Sud , is scheduled to enter service in the second half of 2027 and will be designed to access smaller inland ports, tributaries and canals as well as major rivers. The move comes just weeks after Amer Shipping returned to Concordia Damen for another two 110 m CDS Dry Cargo newbuildings, lifting its programme of shallow-draught vessels to six. Those ships are scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2027 and the second quarter of 2028. The first, AM Lianova , will join Stream Shipping, while the second will enter Amer’s own fleet. Amer Shipping operates a network of close to 60 vessels, transporting around 9m tonnes of cargo annually across the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Germany and Switzerland. Its new partner, Van de Graaf & Meeusen, is a Ridderkerk-based inland shipping and chartering specialist with a fleet of pushboats and barges serving the dry bulk market. TriBarge will operate from Antwerp’s Tweede Havendok, with Devin van Dam joining as a chartering broker on November 1. Another Belgian broker is expected to join in the second quarter of 2027. articles.body: Americas Europe Offshore Fugro lands NOAA seabed mapping contract off Florida Bojan Lepic October 20, 2026 0 32 1 minute read Fugro Fugro Dutch survey specialist Fugro has secured a contract with the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to map about 3,200 sq km of seabed off Florida’s Atlantic coast. The company will conduct hydrographic surveys for NOAA’s Office of Coast Survey, and the resulting data will update nautical charts supporting commercial shipping, government operations, and recreational boating. The work covers a busy coastal region where severe storms, shifting seabed conditions and expanding maritime activity are increasing demand for accurate navigation data. The surveys will also provide information to help monitor coastal changes and protect sensitive marine ecosystems. “Reliable geo-data is essential for safe navigation, efficient maritime operations and understanding how our coastal environments are changing over time,” said Céline Gerson, Fugro’s group director for the Americas. The latest award builds on Fugro’s relationship with NOAA and follows recent hydrographic survey work along Florida’s Gulf Coast. The company has also contributed to the Florida Seafloor Mapping Initiative, mapping more than 56,000 sq km of Florida waters. articles.title: Seaborne coal trade rebounds as Asian energy crisis reshapes global flows
articles.summary: Global seaborne coal trade has returned to growth in 2026, reversing last year’s decline as disruption to LNG supplies and shifting Asian demand patterns reshape international coal flows, according to new research from global shipbroker IFCHOR GALBRAITHS (IG). Seaborne coal exports increased by 3% year-on-year in...
articles.body: Seaborne coal trade rebounds as Asian energy crisis reshapes global flows in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 20/10/2026 Global seaborne coal trade has returned to growth in 2026, reversing last year’s decline as disruption to LNG supplies and shifting Asian demand patterns reshape international coal flows, according to new research from global shipbroker IFCHOR GALBRAITHS (IG). Seaborne coal exports increased by 3% year-on-year in January–September 2026, following a 4% contraction in 2025. The recovery has been driven partly by disruption to LNG shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, prompting Asian power utilities to increase coal purchases. IG’s new Coal Markets Companion Report reveals a market increasingly characterised by divergent regional demand and changing trade routes. Between March and September, Asian seaborne thermal coal imports were broadly flat at around 550 million tonnes, as lower purchases by China (-7%) and India (-10%) were matched by a rise of around 10% in the rest of Asia, led by South Korea, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Japan and Vietnam. Laura Gomez, Research & Advisory, IFCHOR GALBRAITHS, commented: “The recovery in seaborne coal trade is particularly interesting because it is happening despite falling imports into China and India. Demand is shifting towards other Asian markets, partly in response to LNG supply disruption, while changes in sourcing are affecting established trade routes. It demonstrates why we need to look beyond headline coal consumption figures to understand what is happening in seaborne trade.” On the supply side, Indonesia, responsible for approximately 47% of global seaborne thermal coal trade, saw exports fall 7% in January–September, including a 16% decline in the third quarter. IG forecasts Indonesian coal exports easing to approximately 450 million tonnes by 2030. Meanwhile, metallurgical coal followed a different trajectory, with global seaborne trade increasing 10% year-on-year in January–September, supported by stronger Chinese demand. Australian metallurgical coal exports rose 13%, with shipments to China almost doubling. IG launches Coal 360 The findings accompany the launch of Coal 360, IG’s latest Commodities 360 market intelligence service, building on its existing Iron Ore, Agri and Bauxite research. Coal 360 provides detailed analysis of global thermal and metallurgical coal markets, covering production, exports, trade flows, ports, vessel deployment and forecasts, supported by regular updates and access to IG’s Research & Advisory team. articles.body: Fuel Switch Snapshot: LBM nips at LSMGO’s heels in Rotterdam in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 Liquefied biomethane (LBM) is closing in on LSMGO in Rotterdam. Its discounts to LSMGO have narrowed by $100-103/mt to $17-137/mt, depending on engine type. For dual-fuel vessels bunkering in Rotterdam, LBM costs more than HSFO, VLSFO and B100, irrespective of the vessel’s engine type. LBM’s premiums over B100 have narrowed by $16-19/mt to $465-584/mt, as B100 has gained $54/mt and LBM $35-38/mt. The ENGINE-assessed FuelEU Maritime pooling value has risen by €8.90/mtCO2e ($10/mtCO2e) to €95.80/mtCO2e ($108/mtCO2e) over the past week. This has pushed the potential pooling value of LBM’s compliance surplus $31-36/mt higher in the past week. B100’s potential pooling value has also gained $30/mt in the past week. Rotterdam’s B100 has flipped from a $24/mt discount to HSFO to a $26/mt premium over it. B100’s discount to VLSFO in Rotterdam has narrowed by $26/mt to $58/mt. Its discount to LSMGO has narrowed by $119/mt to $602/mt, as LSMGO has dropped by $65/mt and B100 has gained $54/mt. Singapore’s B100 premium over VLSFO has narrowed by $1/mt to $337/mt. Its premium over LSMGO has widened by $15/mt to $44/mt. Liquid fuels Rotterdam’s HSFO and VLSFO prices have gained $4-28/mt over the past week, with VLSFO up the most. Its LSMGO has dropped by $65/mt. Rotterdam’s B100 has gained $54/mt, despite a $30/mt rise in its potential pooling value. B30-VLSFO has risen by $24/mt and B30-LSMGO has dipped by $2/mt in the past week. Singapore’s conventional fuel prices have gained $8-61/mt over the past week, with HSFO up the most. Its B100 has risen by $23/mt. Singapore’s bio-blended bunker sales rose sharply in September, increasing by 43% to 81,000 mt, which was the highest monthly volume since March. The port also recorded B100 bunker sales for a sixth consecutive month, with 2,600 mt sold in September, up from 800 mt in August. Liquid gases Rotterdam’s LNG prices have gained $72-75/mt over the past week depending on engine type. Its LBM prices have gained $35-38/mt. For vessels with Otto medium speed (Otto MS) engines, LBM’s premium over LNG has narrowed by $37/mt to $5/mt. For vessels with diesel slow speed (diesel SS) engines, it has narrowed by $37/mt to $1/mt. Rotterdam LBM’s premiums over VLSFO have widened by $7-10/mt to $407-526/mt. Singapore’s LNG prices have risen by $144-146/mt depending on engine type, as the JKM contract they are priced on has moved from November to December delivery. That move accounts for $146/mt of the rise. Excluding it, LNG (Otto MS) has held level and LNG (diesel SS) has dipped by $1/mt. In Singapore, LNG burnt in diesel SS engines has flipped from a $1/mt discount to LSMGO to a $136/mt premium over it. LNG burnt in Otto MS engines has widened its premium over LSMGO by $138/mt to $193/mt. LNG’s premiums over VLSFO in Singapore have widened by $121-122/mt to $429-486/mt. articles.body: LNG shipping stocks: Down on the surface in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 The UP World LNG Shipping Index fell 6.97 points (3.0%) to close at 224.91, pulled down by a broad equity-market selloff — the S&P 500 lost 1.95%, its biggest weekly drop since June. But the sector’s internals were far stronger than the headline: the median constituent fell just 0.43%, and the weighted index (wUPI) actually rose 2.87%, so the decline was concentrated in a few heavier names rather than reflecting genuine sector weakness. Breadth was 10:11 on above-average volume. Two Asian names led with double-digit gains — MISC +15.4% (fleet expansion with QatarEnergy and a 20-year Petronas newbuild order) and Pan Ocean +11% (breaking through all key resistance) — while the oil & gas majors surged to fresh highs: BP +8.6%, Shell +6.5% and Chevron +6.14%. The drag came from COSCO, down almost 15%, with FLEX LNG and Dynagas each off 8% and Golar −5.6%. In the background, gas markets stayed volatile and bullish: Asian prices reached $29.30/MMBtu, and European prices hit their highest since December 2022 on Hormuz tanker attacks and strong cross-basin competition, with Morgan Stanley lifting its winter TTF forecast to €90/MWh. Spot tanker rates held at $20,500 (Atlantic) and eased to $27,000 (Pacific). UPI & SPX The UP World LNG Shipping Index, which tracks 21 listed LNG shipping companies, lost 6.97 points (3.0%) to close at 224.91 points, while the S&P 500 index lost 1.95%. The chart below illustrates the performance of both indices with weekly data. Week 42-2026: Chart of the UP World LNG Shipping Index with S&P 500 (Source: UP-Indices) Broader View Negative sentiment in equity markets affected the UPI, as shown by the UPI and S&P 500 charts. The median change in the UPI was -0.43 per cent, whilst the weighted index (wUPI) rose by 2.87 per cent. Taken together, these figures do not indicate particularly negative sentiment. The ratio of rising to falling index components was 10:11. Trading volume was above average, with above-average levels seen among both rising and falling stocks. The gas market remains volatile, fuelled by rising European purchases. The Reuters weekly summary, on which the rest of this section is based, states that Asian gas prices rose due to both repeated Iranian attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz and increasing European demand. The average Asian price reached $29.30/mmBtu. Despite an increase in transits via the Strait of Hormuz since September, as well as loadings at Qatar’s Ras Laffan facility, continued attacks on tankers and uncertainty over safe passage are keeping prices supported, he said. “With the disruption likely to persist into winter, competition for flexible LNG supply remains an important bullish factor,” said Arturo Regalado, senior LNG analyst at Kpler. Some tankers continue to leave the Gulf, but the situation remains volatile, said Alex Froley, senior LNG analyst at data intelligence firm ICIS. “The competition between Europe and Asia for flexible cargoes remains strong, as evidenced by increased mid-Atlantic course-change activity,” he added. The LNG tanker Shra’ouh, which was heading round Africa towards India, changed course back north, signalling a destination in the UK, but has recently turned south again, likely bound for Asia, Froley said. Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus, said Asian demand has been supported, with Chinese and South Korean buyers entering the market for spot cargoes, boosting competition between basins and driving European gas prices higher. In Europe, gas prices hovered around €88.57 per megawatt hour (MWh), or $29.20/mmBtu, on Friday afternoon, their highest intraday level since December 2022. “Even with recent warm weather and a recovery in Gulf LNG flows to 30 per cent of pre-conflict levels, our European region will still enter winter with storage at a record low of 74 per cent,” said Morgan Stanley analysts in a report. Morgan Stanley raised its winter TTF forecast to €90/MWh this week and said it could reach €135/MWh due to a combination of a prolonged outage in Qatar, colder weather or other LNG disruptions. S&P Global Energy assessed its daily Northwest Europe LNG price benchmark for cargoes delivered in November on an ex-ship basis at $27.825/mmBtu on Thursday, a $0.580/mmBtu discount to the front-month price at the Dutch TTF gas hub. Spot rates for LNG tankers remained at $20,500 per day for the Atlantic, whilst for the Pacific they fell to $27,000 per day, according to Spark Commodities. Constituents There were also two instances of double-digit growth, both in Asia. The larger of the two was recorded by Malaysia’s MISC (KLSE: 3816), which expanded its LNG fleet with a new tanker in October (under a contract with QatarEnergy) and has this year placed an order with Chinese shipyards for five new vessels under a 20-year contract with Petronas. Delivery is expected in 2030. According to TA, the strong 15.4 per cent rise in its share price took it out of a sideways range to its spring highs, closing just below its highest closing price without forming a wick at higher prices. Trading volume was slightly above average. The second company to post double-digit growth was South Korea’s Pan Ocean (KRX: 028670), which gained 11 per cent. During the week, however, its growth (in the short term) reached as high as 30 per cent. In any case, it has broken through all resistance levels, including key levels, and is continuing towards its pre-pandemic ranges. The next three major gains, of 8 per cent and 6 per cent, share a common thread, as they all relate to the oil and gas trio: BP (NYSE: BP; +8.6 per cent) easily broke through resistance (incidentally, the same level as in 2018), with the closing price and the high for the day being almost identical. Trading volume was slightly above average. Chevron (NYSE: CVX; +6.14 per cent) performed similarly, reaching new all-time highs. Shell (NYSE: SHEL) broke through resistance as early as the beginning of September and has now recorded a clear gain of 6.5 per cent. In its case, too, these are all-time highs. ALNG (OSE: ALNG) gained 1.5 per cent but continues to trade sideways. Given the company’s transformation from a pure transport operator (two TFDE LNG tankers on the spot market) to a gas trader with transport capacity, we expect a change in trend only once this transformation is complete. Exmar (EBR: EXM; +2.2 per cent) is undergoing a similarly subtle transformation, expanding its operations across the entire value chain from upstream to downstream. The share price is trading sideways. Other movements were less than 0.8 per cent. Korea Line Corporation (KRX: 005880) made an unsuccessful attempt to break out of its sideways range. Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (TSE: 9104) fared slightly better; while its attempt to break above the key resistance level was also unsuccessful, it closed above the range’s closing-price resistance level. “K” Line (TSE: 9107), on the other hand, closed within the range. All three Japanese companies – we’ll come back to NYK Line later – are trading within a sideways range at the highest price levels. This brings us to the falling companies. COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation (SS: 600026) suffered the heaviest losses, falling by almost 15 per cent. The chart remains unclear for now. The current uptrend was halted – and perhaps ended – after reaching spring levels. In any case, the price is now below spring levels. It was also the only double-digit decline. Flex LNG (NYSE: FLNG) and Dynagas LNG Partners (NYSE: DLNG) fell by 8 per cent. FLNG closed below the support level of its sideways range for the first time this year, suggesting a breakout. It reached the upper boundary of the previous sideways range’s high prices, but is also near the magnetic support level of the higher range. Given its high cash reserves, dividend payments are not at risk in the foreseeable future, so there is currently no reason for a sustained decline – apart from the general fall in share prices. DLNG fell to its lowest price level since 2024; trading volume was above average for both stocks. Golar LNG (NASDAQ: GLNG; -5.6 per cent) also fell below its support level. This time, on higher volume, it also breached the magnetic support level. Excelerate Energy (NYSE: EE) and New Fortress Energy (NASDAQ: NFE) both fell by four per cent. EE bounced off its support level after the decline, then rose slightly. The current trend is therefore sideways. NFE also showed a corrective decline, yet it has reached new lows. Nakilat (QSE: QGTS) closed near the previous week’s close, supported by a higher open. The company, affected by geopolitical tensions, thus lost only 1.8 per cent. This brings us to NYK Line (TSE: 9101), which fell 1.3% while trading in the upper range of its sideways channel on below-average volume. Capital Clean Energy Carriers (NASDAQ: CCEC) fell 1%, trading near the support level of its two-year sideways range. ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADX: ADNOCLS) remains at its major resistance level, down 0.9% after the rise the week before last. Tsakos Energy Navigation (NYSE: TEN) also fell 0.4 per cent after failing to break above resistance at its all-time high. It therefore remains within a short-term sideways range. The failed breakout appears linked more to the stock market decline than to a waning appetite for the company, given the above-average daily volume during the upward breakout. However, the following days saw the aforementioned return to the range. Crystal Ball Qatar remains sidelined among the conflict’s losers — but the key constraint is export, not production. The damage to Ras Laffan removed around 17% of capacity (two of 14 trains), which QatarEnergy expects to take three to five years to repair. The remaining ~80% of capacity is intact and could, in principle, return to market — but the Strait of Hormuz is Qatar’s sole export route, and executives (including Shell’s) caution that even a reopening would not restore pre-war flows overnight, as high war-risk insurance continues to deter tanker returns to the Gulf. For now, this keeps a large share of Qatari volume bottled up, and US LNG exporters emerge as the clear winners. European importers were shielded from spot price increases largely because of long-term US contracts; however, these are not enough to replenish winter inventories, and European companies must return to the market despite Qatar’s continuing export restrictions. We expect most of the rising US gas production to flow toward Europe. New global LNG producers should also benefit, as energy source diversification becomes more important than ever — provided importing economies remain healthy enough to absorb higher energy costs. The outlook remains volatile, but positive in the long term. The gradual phasing out of steam vessels and the addition of new liquefaction capacity will continue to drive the sector forward. articles.title: The Grande Island: What you delete is only half the story
articles.summary: The recent decision in Olam International Ltd v Pacific Basin Supramax Ltd (The Grande Island) [2026] EWHC 2136 (Comm) concerned a familiar feature of charter partynegotiations where standard wording had been incorporated but parts of it deliberately deleted. The question was what those deletions meant for the...
articles.body: The Grande Island: What you delete is only half the story in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 The recent decision in Olam International Ltd v Pacific Basin Supramax Ltd (The Grande Island) [2026] EWHC 2136 (Comm) concerned a familiar feature of charter partynegotiations where standard wording had been incorporated but parts of it deliberately deleted. The question was what those deletions meant for the provisions left behind. Background The Grande Island was chartered under an amended NYPE form for a trip from Ghent to Nigeria. The charter party incorporated the BIMCO Piracy Clause for Time Charter Parties 2013, but sub-clauses 81(a) and (b) were expressly deleted. Had it remained, Clause 81(a) would have given Owners a broad right, based on the reasonable judgement of Owners or the Master, to refuse to proceed to or through an area considered dangerous because of piracy, or to leave such an area. Clause 81 (b) dealt with the alternative orders to be given by Charterers following the exercise of that right. Furthermore, Clause 81(c) was retained, and it allowed Owners, where the vessel proceeded to or through an area exposed to piracy risk, to take reasonable preventative measures to protect the vessel, crew and cargo. The clause gave examples of such measures, including re-routing, proceeding in convoy and adjusting speed or course, but this list was not exhaustive. After arriving off Warri, the vessel was unable to berth. Considering the background of piracy risk in the area, she left Warri and returned towards Lagos, before returning to Warri around three days later. The dispute was whether that temporary departure was permitted under Clause 81(c) and therefore whether the vessel remained on hire. Charterers’ case Charterers’ position centred on the parties’ decision to delete Clause 81(a) and (b). In their view, this was important because Clause 81(a) contained their express right for Owners to leave an area on account of piracy risk. Having specifically removed that right, Charterers argued that the more general wording of Clause 81(c) should not be interpreted as giving it back. They also relied on the types of preventative measures identified in Clause 81(c). Charterers argued that those examples were consistent with measures taken while navigating through or operating in the relevant area rather than leaving it altogether. On that construction, the vessel’s return towards Lagos was outside the protection of Clause 81(c) with Charterers maintaining that hire should not be payable for the concerned period. Owners’ case Owners’ case was that the deleted and retained provisions served different purposes. Clauses 81(a) and (b) provided broader rights, including a right triggered by the reasonable judgement of Owners or the Master. Clause 81(c) was narrower, requiring actual exposure to piracy risk, with any preventative measure taken also having to satisfy an objective standard of reasonableness. As such, the deletion of the broader rights did not mean that the parties had also removed the separate protection available under Clause 81(c). Furthermore, Owners relied on the breadth of the wording used in that provision and the fact that the listed preventative measures were examples rather than an exhaustive list. What did the Court decide? The arbitral tribunal found in Owners’ favour. It was satisfied that there was a piracy risk at Warri and that temporarily leaving the area was a reasonable preventative measure. Therefore, the vessel remained on hire. Charterers appealed under section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1966, but the Commercial Court upheld the award. The Court considered the retained wording of Clause 81(c) sufficiently clear and broad to encompass leaving the area where doing so amounted to a reasonable preventative measure. The examples appearing in the clause did not confine the wider wording, particularly as the clause made clear that the measures identified were not exhaustive. Importantly, the Court did not treat the deletion of Clause 81(a) and Clause 81(b) as meaningless. Those provisions would have given Owners additional and more extensive rights. As a result, removing them changed the parties’ bargain but it did not narrow the separate right they had chosen to retain under Clause 81(c). Practical considerations for Charterers From a Charterers’ perspective, the case illustrates why amendments should be tested against the charter party as a whole. Removing one contractual right may not achieve the intended result if another provision can authorise similar conduct under a different test. This is particularly relevant where standard wording sits alongside bespoke rider clauses, as similar or overlapping rights may operate independently of each other. The treatment of the examples in Clause 81(c) is also worth noting. Where a contractual provision contains a broad right followed by a non-exhaustive list of examples, Charterers should be cautious about assuming that the right is confined to the situations expressly listed. If the parties intend the permitted measures to be limited to particular actions, clear wording may be required. At the fixture stage, the question should therefore not stop at what is being deleted. Charterers should also consider what rights remain and how they interact. If the commercial intention is that Owners should not be permitted to take a particular step, or that hire should cease if they do, it may be preferrable to address that consequence expressly. The decision is equally useful when a claim arises. If Owners rely on a safety or security clause to justify a diversion or other action, Charterers should focus on the particular requirements of that specific clause and the evidence supporting them. Here, the retained right depended on actual exposure to piracy risk and on the measure taken being reasonable. Those are matters capable of factual scrutiny, including what the risk was at the relevant time, what information was available to Owners and the Master, what alternatives were reasonably available and why the particular course was selected. Before making an off-hire deduction, Charterers should consider the charter party as a whole. Where another provision permits Owners to take the relevant action and expressly addresses the resulting allocation of time or hire, that provision may determine the position irrespective of the general off hire regime. Concluding, the drafting lesson from the Grande Island is a simple one. When negotiating what comes out of a charter party, equal attention should be paid to what stays in. Source: West of England 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The question was what those deletions meant for the provisions left behind.
Background The Grande Island was chartered under an amended NYPE form for a trip from Ghent to Nigeria.

articles.body: Korea seeks dedicated US visa quota for shipbuilding workers in Shipbuilding News 20/10/2026 Korea is seeking a dedicated U.S. visa quota for shipbuilding workers as a condition for carrying out its $150 billion investment commitment under the Make American Shipbuilding Great Again (MASGA) initiative, according to the information submitted to Rep. Huh Sung-moo of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy. On Monday, Huh said that information he had received from the ministry indicated that it has been “explaining” to its U.S. counterparts the conditions “Washington needs to meet for Korea to fulfill its investment commitment.” “In particular, we have requested that the U.S. provide sufficient shipbuilding orders, allow joint shipbuilding through exemptions from restrictions on overseas construction, offer financial incentives and establish a dedicated visa quota for shipbuilding workers as prerequisites for implementing the investment commitment,” the ministry said in its response. The Korean government and business associations have been pushing for the introduction of a new E-4 visa category for Korean professionals in specialty occupations, but the proposal has yet to be enacted into law. In a separate response to Huh’s inquiry about whether the proposed shipbuilding visa quota would be separated from the E-4 visa, the ministry said it has “not made a specific request, but we believe that professional workers covered by the existing visa proposal and skilled technical workers needed at shipyards are different categories of workers.” “The number of workers needed will vary depending on the timing and progress of each investment project,” the ministry said. “At this stage, we believe establishing a visa route for workers to enter the U.S. is more important than specifying a number.” In a separate statement, the industry ministry said: “Led by the foreign ministry, Korea is discussing ways to improve the visa system to facilitate the entry and stay of Korean corporate personnel, including those in the shipbuilding sector.” The push for a dedicated visa quota for shipbuilding workers is key, as the sector accounts for $150 billion of Korea’s $350 billion investment commitment to the U.S., making it the largest single segment in the package. Compared with other areas of investment, shipbuilding offers more clearly defined areas of cooperation under a structure where Korean shipbuilders can directly benefit. To help revitalize the U.S. shipbuilding industry, skilled Korean workers will need to be deployed to American shipyards in the early stages to transfer their expertise and know-how. Personnel exchanges are also essential because the cooperation covers not only shipbuilding operations but also joint research and development projects. Currently, the Partner with Korea Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Young Kim, is pending in Congress. The bill seeks to establish a new visa category for Korean nationals working in specialty occupations, with an annual quota of up to 15,000 visas. Although versions of the bill have been introduced in successive sessions of Congress for more than a decade, it has yet to make significant progress. Even if the legislation advances, the quota would have to be shared across professions, potentially leaving insufficient slots for workers in shipbuilding. This appears to be one reason Korea is pushing for a separate, dedicated visa quota for the sector. “To maximize the benefits of the MASGA project, additional institutional measures are required,” Huh said. “Effective support measures, including visa negotiations, should be pursued to ensure that Korean workers can be employed at U.S. shipyards without difficulty.” Source: The Korea Times 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: China unexpectedly increases its purchases of Brazilian oil in Freight News 20/10/2026 According to the South China Morning Post , amidst the turmoil in the global energy supply chain due to the conflict in the Gulf region, the Brazilian economy has seized a golden opportunity. According to a report by the Brazil-China Trade Council, bilateral trade reached a record high of $143 billion in the first nine months of the year. Brazilian crude oil exports to China hit a record high. A quarterly analysis based on official government data shows that the financial situation of this South American economy is very positive. Specifically, in the first nine months of the year, Brazil’s exports to China increased by 12%, reaching $84.7 billion . Conversely, imports of goods from China to Brazil also recorded an increase of nearly 10%, reaching $58.6 billion . The two-way trade deficit generated a trade surplus of $26.1 billion in just nine months, accounting for 42% of Brazil’s total trade surplus with the rest of the world . Crude oil contributed to these record-breaking figures, with exports to China surging 49% to a record $21.8 billion . This boom was driven by two main factors: increased shipping volumes and rising prices, both 27% and 17% respectively. China now holds half of Brazil’s total crude oil exports, nearly seven times the market share of India , the second-largest buyer. Despite international market fluctuations, Chinese customs data cited by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that China aggressively purchased oil from Brazil, even as its total crude oil imports fell by 32% in the second quarter. This strategic shift boosted Brazil’s total global crude oil exports by nearly 29%, reaching $43 billion . Not only China, but Brazil’s oil sales to India also saw a phenomenal 165% increase. The boom in the energy market has created a major shift in Brazil’s total export value. Reports show that oil now accounts for nearly 26% of the country’s total exports to China, up 6.3 percentage points from the previous year, and second only to its main export item, soybeans (which account for over 35%). Growth is slowing down. Besides the aforementioned export records, the figures for the first nine months of the year also show that Brazil’s export growth to China is slowing down. Specifically, this growth has slowed since the Council reported in July, when exports to China recorded a 22% increase. In contrast to the booming energy market, the beef market recorded a decline, negatively impacting Brazil’s revenue. Specifically, the country’s beef exports fell by 8.5%, to $5.5 billion , accompanied by a 22% decrease in volume. This was due to Brazil reaching its annual quota of 1.1 million tons under protectionist regulations from the Chinese market. According to the report, China dropped to fifth place among countries buying Brazilian beef in September, accounting for only 5.6% of total consumption, behind the US with a market share of 21.5%. Conversely, electric vehicles were the biggest driver of Brazil’s import growth from China. The country’s purchases of plug-in hybrid vehicles increased by 89%, reaching $2.87 billion , while battery-powered electric vehicles saw a 341% increase, reaching approximately $2.4 billion . Conventional hybrid vehicles currently account for about one-tenth of Brazil’s total vehicle imports from China. Brazilian brands hold 86% of the electric vehicle market share that Brazil imports from overseas. In response to significant market fluctuations, BYD – China’s largest automaker in Brazil – proactively shipped large consignments ahead of the surge in demand and began assembling electric vehicles directly at its factory in Camaçari, Bahia state. Besides the aforementioned key products, the report also noted the initial positive results of the Chinese market’s opening to Brazilian agricultural products. Specifically, revenue from sorghum reached $170 million , with the Chinese market currently consuming 95% of Brazil’s total sorghum exports. Simultaneously, exports of spodumene, a lithium-containing mineral, from the South American nation also increased by 339%, reaching $172.3 million , with 97% of production destined for China. articles.title: Supply Constraints Keep Asian Coal Prices High
articles.summary: Asian thermal coal prices are likely to stay elevated in the near term as Indonesian supply uncertainty and lower Chinese production limit supply, says Fitch Ratings. Demand from gas-to-coal switching in Japan and Korea is likely to stay firm, driven by the Middle East conflict, pushing regional prices higher –...
articles.body: Supply Constraints Keep Asian Coal Prices High in Commodity News 20/10/2026 Asian thermal coal prices are likely to stay elevated in the near term as Indonesian supply uncertainty and lower Chinese production limit supply, says Fitch Ratings. Demand from gas-to-coal switching in Japan and Korea is likely to stay firm, driven by the Middle East conflict, pushing regional prices higher – particularly for high- Calorific Value (CV) coal. Firmer prices will support miners’ near-term cash flow and debt-servicing capacity, but not reverse longer-term pressure from declining Chinese and Indian import requirements and the energy transition. Rising regulatory uncertainty and higher cash costs for Indonesian miners partly offsets the benefit of stronger prices. Higher prices in Indonesia may ease pressure for government imposing deeper production cuts, but uncertainty over production quota allocation for 2027, single-door export policy, domestic market obligation requirements, and broader mining regulation will continue to constrain operating visibility. Indonesian export supply is likely to remain difficult to predict despite the government easing its (initially) much lower 2026 production coal output target of 600 million tonnes (2025: actual output 790 million). This was compounded by severe drought from El Nino which has restricted barging at Barito River, contributing to export declines of 23.3% yoy in August and 18.1% in September. Some Indonesian coal producers have declared force majeure on coal-supply shipments due to an inability to secure mining quotas, and logistical bottlenecks. Chinese coal supply should recover as tighter safety inspections following May’s Shanxi mine accident ease gradually. National raw-coal output fell 10.1% yoy in July and 7.7% in August, leaving output down 3.3% in the first eight months of 2026,and Shanxi down 12.5%. Imports filled the domestic shortfall in part, with stronger Mongolian shipments helping to offset weaker supply from Indonesia. Chinese demand, which accounted for over one-third of Asian seaborne thermal-coal imports in 2025, should provide limited support once domestic production normalises. Thermal generation rose only 0.9% in the first eight months of 2026, down 3.5% in July and 4.3% in August as renewable and nuclear output rose. We expect thermal generation to be broadly flat or to decline mildly in 2027 as new renewable capacity meets incremental power demand, although weather conditions and renewable curtailment remain uncertainties. Weak steel and construction-material demand will also weigh on consumption, offset partly by growth in coal-to-chemicals. High gas prices should have limited implications for Chinese coal demand because gas-fired generation accounts for only a small share of the power mix. Chinese demand is likely to remain subdued despite Asia-Pacific coal import demand continuing to receive support from South & South-East (S&SEA) Asia markets. S&SEA coal demand remains robust, supported by 5%-7% power demand growth, weaker hydropower output, and transmission constraints on renewable additions. India and Vietnam are driving growth, while energy-security concerns are reinforcing coal’s role in regional power systems. Higher prices will support miners’ earnings, cash flow and debt-servicing capacity, particularly for low-cost producers with strong balance sheets. Fitch expects prices to remain firm for the next few months, supported by winter restocking. Qinhuangdao 5,500 kcal/kg thermal coal exceeded CNY1,000/tonne in early October despite seasonally weak demand. For Indonesian producers, however, rising regulatory risk reduces operating visibility, becoming a more important credit consideration alongside commodity prices. Recovering Chinese production should eventually ease prices, but timing will depend on outside supply. Continued Indonesian production restraints or logistics disruption could keep the seaborne market tighter in the near term, even as lower Chinese and Indian import requirements and the energy transition weaken the longer-term export outlook. Yet stronger prices are also unlikely to alter longer-term diversification away from thermal coal, with producers investing in other commodities to broaden cash flow diversification. Source: Fitch Ratings 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: SSE Picks Seaway7 for Berwick Bank B Offshore Wind Foundations and Cables Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 (Credit: SSE) SSE Renewables has selected Subsea7's Seaway7 as preferred supplier for offshore wind turbine foundations and subsea inter-array cables at its 1.4 GW Berwick Bank B offshore wind project in Scotland, under an agreement expected to support 465 UK jobs. The preferred supplier agreement covers engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) of approximately 90 fixed-bottom turbine foundations, as well as the design, supply and installation of inter-array cables. The project is planned for the outer Firth of Forth, approximately 38 kilometers off the Scottish Borders coastline, with water depths averaging 52 meters and reaching up to 59.7 meters. According to SSE, Berwick Bank B would become the world's deepest fixed-bottom offshore wind farm upon completion. Seaway7 plans to deploy three installation vessels for the offshore campaign: Seaway Alfa Lift, Seaway Strashnov and Seaway Phoenix. The appointment remains subject to a final contract award and a final investment decision (FID) by SSE, expected in late 2027. If approved, preparatory offshore construction work could begin in 2028, with foundation and inter-array cable installation scheduled to start in 2029 and finish in 2031. The agreement is expected to support 465 jobs across the UK, including 400 in Scotland. These comprise approximately 160 direct roles at Seaway7, 105 indirect jobs in the UK supply chain and a further 200 direct and indirect positions associated with foundation marshalling activities at a Scottish port yet to be announced. "We are proud to have been selected by SSE Renewables as the preferred supplier for Berwick Bank B and to continue a relationship that has successfully delivered major offshore wind projects including Beatrice, Seagreen and Dogger Bank. All three rates cover dry, refrigerated and special equipment. articles.title: US moves to legitimise shadow tanker fleet
articles.summary: The Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers to approved investors who would refurbish the vessels and return them to legitimate crude trades, US energy secretary Chris Wright revealed yesterday, as Washington scrambles to contain soaring freight costs amid the Hormuz crisis. Speaking at...
articles.body: Americas Europe Regulatory Tankers US moves to legitimise shadow tanker fleet Sam Chambers October 20, 2026 0 916 2 minutes read Greenpeace Greenpeace The Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers to approved investors who would refurbish the vessels and return them to legitimate crude trades, US energy secretary Chris Wright revealed yesterday, as Washington scrambles to contain soaring freight costs amid the Hormuz crisis. Speaking at a Citadel Securities event in New York, Wright said the government was developing an approval process for formerly blacklisted vessels to trade under recognised owners, carrying only non-sanctioned oil. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’” he said. Wright insisted the move was not a blanket lifting of sanctions on Iranian or Russian oil, describing it instead as the conversion of ships into legitimate assets. He put the global dark fleet at around 1,600 tankers and suggested “dozens” or possibly “hundreds” might eventually re-enter compliant trading. Tanker owners’ association INTERTANKO has pushed back hard, warning that legalising a vessel does not automatically address its condition, ownership or insurance. “If additional tanker capacity is required, policy should encourage cargoes towards the quality, compliant fleet,” the association said. INTERTANKO warned that opaque insurance arrangements, weak oversight and missing inspection histories pose risks to crews, the environment and coastal states, while sending the wrong signal to owners that have invested heavily in safety and compliance. Market analysts are equally sceptical about whether the initiative can meaningfully depress extraordinary freight rates. Kpler estimates only 24 of roughly 160 OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs could realistically return to mainstream trading after ownership and age restrictions are considered. It argued yesterday that war risk around the Middle East Gulf, rather than vessel numbers alone, is driving freight costs, and that loosening sanctions could weaken geopolitical leverage without delivering meaningful relief.\ Braemar put the potential increase even lower at just 19 VLCCs once vessels tied to Iran and European sanctions are excluded. Braemar stressed that any lasting impact depends on Hormuz flows and how long Washington’s approval arrangements remain in place. Arrow Research’s filtering has produced a maximum of 22 eligible tankers across all sizes, including 14 VLCCs, and none in the suezmax or aframax segments. Arrow sees continued upside risk for freight, with the strong market potentially extending through the first quarter of 2027 as shuttle operations, ship-to-ship transfers and security risks keep tonnage tied up. BRS, meanwhile, has identified 148 deepsea tankers sanctioned by the US alone, representing just 2.5% of the global deepsea fleet. Only 14 appear to have been idle for more than three months. Most of the remainder are already working in grey trades, while UK and EU restrictions could prevent them obtaining essential insurance and other maritime services. BRS maintained that Washington’s initiative is unlikely to have a significant immediate impact on freight rates, with the majority of potentially eligible tonnage already employed and the fundamental constraints on tanker movements through Hormuz remaining unresolved. The shadow fleet move follows Washington’s decision earlier this month to temporarily authorise Russian diesel trade until April 7, 2027, drawing criticism from Kyiv and US lawmakers. articles.title: Northern Sea Route smashes shipping records again
articles.summary: Shipping along Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) has already broken last year’s transit record. New figures from Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) show 104 confirmed transits by September 30, surpassing the 103 recorded during the whole of 2025 and 97 in 2024. articles.body: Asia Dry Cargo Europe Operations Tankers Northern Sea Route smashes shipping records again Sam Chambers October 20, 2026 1 244 2 minutes read Sovcomflot Sovcomflot Shipping along Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) has already broken last year’s transit record. New figures from Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) show 104 confirmed transits by September 30, surpassing the 103 recorded during the whole of 2025 and 97 in 2024. Estimated transit cargo reached 3.7m tonnes, up 15% on the whole of last year, while the combined deadweight of vessels using the route increased 26% to 7.8m dwt. The final tally could be considerably higher. CHNL identified another 45 potential transits already underway or within the route at the end of September, suggesting the season could approach 150 voyages and more than 4.5m tonnes of cargo. Tankers have been the biggest cargo contributors, with 22 eastbound voyages carrying approximately 2.1m tonnes, predominantly Russian crude heading for Asia. Bulk carriers accounted for another 1.1m tonnes of eastbound cargo, while considerable westbound activity involved ships repositioning from Asia towards European Russia. The route is also attracting growing interest from international operators. Four direct Asia-Europe voyages had been completed by September 30, compared with just one during the whole of last year. Russian energy exports are providing much of the momentum. Russian oil exports through the NSR have climbed nearly 50% this year, with approximately 20m barrels shipped to Asia between July and mid-October. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal and Black Sea has made the expensive and potentially hazardous Arctic passage increasingly attractive. Russian LNG shipments are also contributing to traffic growth, with CHNL recording four eastbound LNG cargoes totalling approximately 300,000 tonnes. However, the accelerating use of one of the planet’s most environmentally sensitive waterways is raising mounting concerns. Dr Sian Prior, lead advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance, warned in a release from earlier in the year that growing commercial shipping activity would bring “increased climate impacts, increased pollution and increased loss of biodiversity.” The NGO is particularly concerned about black carbon emissions from ships burning fossil fuels. When deposited on snow and ice, the particles accelerate melting by reducing the amount of sunlight reflected away from the surface. Swiss researchers have found that exhaust from a single vessel can alter Arctic cloud formation, potentially accelerating sea-ice melt locally. Scientists from Lausanne’s Swiss Federal Institute of Technology used emissions from their own research ship as a natural experiment. Preliminary estimates suggest that when polluted clouds form above ice, changes in cloud properties can cause around 1 mm of additional melting per day within roughly 100 m. Greater tanker activity also increases the risk of oil spills in remote Arctic waters, where harsh conditions and limited emergency response infrastructure make pollution particularly difficult to contain. articles.title: Rheinmetall and MSC win bid for Mangalia shipyard
articles.summary: Rheinmetall and Swiss container shipping group MSC have won the auction for the Mangalia shipyard in Romania, with the partners planning to develop the site for both civilian and military shipbuilding. The proposed acquisition carries a purchase price of approximately €138 million, which will be paid jointly by...
articles.body: Rheinmetall and Swiss container shipping group MSC have won the auction for the Mangalia shipyard in Romania, with the partners planning to develop the site for both civilian and military shipbuilding. The proposed acquisition carries a purchase price of approximately €138 million, which will be paid jointly by Rheinmetall and MSC. Completion is expected within the coming weeks. Until the transaction closes, the acquisition remains subject to the necessary final procedures. Partners plan dual-use shipbuilding site The partners intend to establish a dual-use production facility at Mangalia, allowing civilian and military shipbuilding projects for Romanian and international customers to be undertaken at the same site. The shipyard will be divided into separate operational sectors and security zones to accommodate the two areas of activity. For Rheinmetall Naval Systems, Mangalia will support the construction of four naval vessels commissioned by the Romanian government. These comprise two 96-metre offshore patrol vessels and two 43-metre diver-support vessels. Rheinmetall also intends to use the site as a hub for additional military shipbuilding programmes, creating capacity for future projects in Southeastern Europe. “Following the acquisition, we plan to expand and upgrade the shipyard comprehensively. Our aim is to further develop the existing infrastructure, improve production conditions and adapt capacity to meet future requirements,” said Tim Wagner, CEO of Rheinmetall’s Naval Systems division. “This will enable the site in the long term to play a key role in the implementation of our strategic activities in Southeastern Europe and to strengthen our industrial presence in the region,” he added. Rheinmetall has operated in Romania since 2024 through Rheinmetall Automecanica, based in Mediaș. Mangalia is located on Romania’s Black Sea coast, south of Constanța. MSC’s participation will support the civilian shipbuilding component of the planned dual-use facility.

articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd introduces new SE5 service in Far East–Europe network reshuffle
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has announced a series of changes to its Far East–Europe network under the Gemini Cooperation, including the introduction of a new Asia South Europe 5 (SE5) service. The adjustments will begin in November 2026 and affect six services connecting Asia with Northern Europe and the Mediterranean. The changes...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd has announced a series of changes to its Far East–Europe network under the Gemini Cooperation, including the introduction of a new Asia South Europe 5 (SE5) service. The adjustments will begin in November 2026 and affect six services connecting Asia with Northern Europe and the Mediterranean. The changes include revised port rotations, additional calls and improved connections through key Mediterranean hubs. New SE5 service connects Asia with Western Mediterranean The new SE5 service will provide direct connections from Central and South China to the Western Mediterranean, serving Algeciras in Spain and Tangier Med in Morocco. The service will also offer onward connections to West Africa through Tangier. Its port rotation will be: Shanghai – Xiamen – Tanjung Pelepas – Suez Canal – Algeciras – Tangier Med – Algeciras – Suez Canal – Xiamen The first vessel will be Maersk Edirne , voyage 647W, scheduled to call at Shanghai on November 22, 2026. Mediterranean services undergo further changes Hapag-Lloyd will also revise its SE1, SE2, SE3 and SE4 services. The SE1 service will replace its Algeciras call with westbound and eastbound calls at Port Said. Colombo will also be added to the eastbound rotation, strengthening connections between the Adriatic, Sri Lanka and the wider Asian network. The SE2 service will replace its westbound Tangier call with Port Said and introduce a new westbound call at Salalah. It will continue serving Valencia, Barcelona, La Spezia, Genoa and Vado Ligure. Meanwhile, SE3 will operate a simplified Mediterranean rotation through Port Said and Damietta. Its eastbound Colombo call will be discontinued. The SE4 service will add Nansha in South China and remove Shanghai from its rotation. It will also introduce a westbound call at Damietta, alongside its existing Port Said connection. These changes will strengthen links between Asian export markets and Mediterranean ports while expanding connections through regional hubs. Rotterdam becomes first European call on NE1 Hapag-Lloyd will also revise its North Europe Express 1 (NE1) service. Under the new rotation, Rotterdam will become the first European port of call, while Tangier will be removed. The revised service will operate through Ningbo, Shanghai, Tanjung Pelepas, Rotterdam, Wilhelmshaven, Bremerhaven, Rotterdam, Salalah and Singapore. The first affected vessel will be Moscow Maersk , voyage 646W, scheduled to call at Ningbo on November 13, 2026. The network adjustments will be introduced progressively from mid-November, with individual services transitioning according to their announced vessel schedules.

articles.body: CMA CGM has announced higher Freight All Kind (FAK) rates for shipments from Asia to the Mediterranean and North Africa, alongside new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on other trade routes. The revised FAK rates will apply from November 1 to 14, 2026. Rates for 40-foot containers will reach US$7,100 on shipments to North Africa. The carrier has also announced surcharges for cargo moving from the west coast of South America and from Northern Europe to North Africa. New FAK rates from Asia The new rates cover shipments from major Asian ports to the Western Mediterranean, Adriatic, Eastern Mediterranean, Black Sea and North Africa. Destination 20-foot container 40-foot / 40-foot HC West Mediterranean US$3,900 US$4,900 Adriatic US$4,000 US$5,000 East Mediterranean US$4,200 US$5,200 Black Sea US$4,200 US$5,200 North Africa US$5,300 US$7,100 The rates cover dry, refrigerated, out-of-gauge and paying empty containers. They include basic freight, bunker-related surcharges, Emissions Trading System (ETS) charges and Low Sulphur Surcharges (LSS). However, terminal handling charges, safety and security fees, and other local charges may apply separately. Additional surcharges on other routes From November 1, CMA CGM will introduce a PSS of US$150 per container for dry cargo shipped from the west coast of South America. The surcharge will cover shipments to the eastern coasts of Central America and Mexico, the Caribbean, the Leeward and Windward Islands, and the east coast of South America. It will also apply to cargo bound for Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Separately, CMA CGM will apply a surcharge of €150 per TEU on shipments from Northern Europe to North Africa, starting November 7. The charge will cover all cargo types. Spain and Portugal are excluded from the origin range, while Morocco is excluded from the destination range. The carrier noted that additional bunker, terminal handling and other applicable charges may apply to shipments covered by the new PSS measures.

REUTERS/Khalil Ashawi By Ari Natter and Annmarie Hordern (Bloomberg) — The Trump administration is authorizing the sale of sanctioned oil tankers in an effort to allow the vessels to start legitimately shipping crude, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. The US government is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use the ships to transport non-sanctioned oil, Wright said Monday at a Citadel Securities event in New York. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’ ” Wright said. “They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore.” Wright’s comments represent the first detailed public explanation from the Trump administration about turning to sanctioned tankers as it seeks to expand the number of ships available to transport crude and boost supply disrupted by the war in Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Trump administration is undertaking an approval process to grant ships legitimate status, Wright said. He rejected the idea that the US was simply removing sanctions from tankers that carried crude from nations such as Russia or Iran. “We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers,” Wright said. “There is no removing of sanctions.” The move comes as Republicans in the US confront voters who are concerned about higher fuel costs weeks before midterm elections. Gasoline and diesel prices surged following the Mideast conflict adding a pain point for voters already worried about affordability. Wright estimated that there are about 1,600 vessels in the global “dark fleet” of sanctioned tankers. The Trump administration’s effort to convert those into lawful ships could ultimately add “dozens” or even “hundreds” of tankers to the legitimate fleet, he said. The perils of transporting oil through the strait have sent shipping fees skyrocketing. Moving oil from the Persian Gulf to East Asia costs more than six times as much as it did prior to the conflict. More than 40% of the world’s fleet of about 850 very large crude carriers are now either in the Persian Gulf or within a couple of days sailing time from it, according to Signal Ocean, a shipping data provider. In addition, Wright said during the wide-ranging interview that part of the reason the Trump administration agreed to work with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release the country’s diesel supplies into global markets in a widely criticized move was to provide an incentive for the Kremlin to end the war with Ukraine. “If you can produce more diesel than you consume, you can export it to the world. Well, what’s their route to do that? They can they can end the conflict in Ukraine,” Wright said. “That would be a real plus. They could get an energy ceasefire with the Ukrainians and fix their refineries, or they can reduce their consumption of diesel for war fighting activities. So if they change their behavior, and all of these are steps towards peace in the conflict, and you have surplus diesel, where you can export it to the world.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Recent Changes in U.S. At-Sea Interdiction of Illicit Narcotics
articles.summary: Sometime back in the fall of 2025, I was contacted by a prominent national television, radio, and print news reporter with a surprising (but understandable under the circumstances) request for background information to inform her reporting.
articles.body: Recent Changes in U.S. At-Sea Interdiction of Illicit Narcotics Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Jeffrey Lewis , Contributor Jeffrey Lewis is a member at Cozen O’Connor and has over 30 years of extensive... October 19, 2026 Crewmembers from Coast Guard Station South Padre Island practice interdiction techniques with a 33-foot high-speed law enforcement boat and a 30-foot small boat. The station received three of these high-speed boats to enhance the unit's law enforcement capabilities. This style of 30-foot small boat is commonly used by drug smugglers and fishermen illegally dropping nets in U.S. waters. USCG photo by PA2 Adam Egger Sometime back in the fall of 2025, I was contacted by a prominent national television, radio, and print news reporter with a surprising (but understandable under the circumstances) request for background information to inform her reporting. She was working on a story covering the numerous lethal military strikes on alleged drug trafficking speedboats (lanchas) in international waters and the waters of Central and South American countries that we all were seeing and hearing about in the news. The reporter’s core question for me? Paraphrasing: We see how the military is conducting these operations now; how did it work before? It was and is an excellent question we all should be asking and the answers to which we as Americans all ought to know and remember, lest our society fall victim to the all-too-human phenomenon of “shifting baselines” — a dynamic akin to relative course plotting, in which we forget where we’ve been and how things once were done because we are only paying attention to what is happening in our immediate vicinity. Not long after my conversation with the reporter, the federal government started seizing oil-laden tank ships departing Venezuela and, not long after that, attacking the Islamic Republic of Iran, predictably grinding commercial transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz to a halt. And so it was that the lancha strikes seemed to be eclipsed by far more concerning events. As far as I can tell, the lancha strikes story I was interviewed for never made it to air or print (although others in the media have since refocused some attention on the issue). Still, I believe it is important to at least speak to the issue of how these military strikes are being executed now (from what little the American public is told) compared with how U.S. at-sea law enforcement interdiction efforts were previously conducted. In breaking this information down, I think the most easily digestible way to present it is with the familiar “Five W’s”: “ Who , What , Where , When , and Why ?” Who Conducts the Interdiction Operations? Historically, at-sea interdiction of illicit drugs has been a federal law enforcement mission conducted by the U.S. Coast Guard, and this is so for at least two important reasons. The first and most important reason is that the Coast Guard stands alone among the U.S. military services as both a branch of our military and a civilian law enforcement agency. Congress intentionally created it that way by statute (see 14 U.S.C. §§ 101 & 102). The other five services (Army, Navy, Marines, Air Force, Space Force) are subject to the Posse Comitatus Act (18 U.S.C. § 1385), under which they are expressly barred from civilian law enforcement activities. The second reason is that the at-sea interdiction mission—whether it be directed at illicit drugs or any other items smuggled into the United States—is at the core of the Coast Guard’s DNA. This goes back to its predecessor agency the Revenue Marine, which was conceived by our first Secretary of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton, and created by the 1st Congress of the United States on August 4, 1790, as a fleet of ten armed cutters that collected tariffs and deterred smuggling along the Atlantic Coast. Recently, beginning on September 1, 2025, the first of as many as 78 (reported numbers range from the 60s to the 70s) separate U.S. lancha strikes was reported in the news, with the most recent strike as of this writing reported to have occurred on September 19, 2026. Media reports are that the Trump administration is conducting these operations through the Department of Defense (DOD) military services, almost entirely with the use of aerial firepower. The deployment of military assets to strike these privately owned foreign boats is predicated on claims by the Trump Administration that the United States is in an armed conflict with Latin American drug cartels, and that the lanchas are carrying illicit cartel drugs bound for the United States. On this basis, the government appears to be justifying its actions as a lawful use of military force. However, a recent United Nations Human Rights Council report, released September 21, 2026, concludes the U.S. military strikes on lanchas are breaches of international law and could constitute crimes against humanity. What Are We Interdicting? Historically, we have always had a very good idea what kinds of contraband the Coast Guard is interdicting because they don’t just tell us, they show us. As a kid growing up on the Gulf Coast in the 1970s and 1980s, the image is burned into my mind of the Coast Guard captain and crew, just back from an enforcement operation, posing at the dock with bails upon bails of illicit narcotics confiscated at sea. It was in the local papers and on the nightly news shows every time you turned around. Those confiscated narcotics are critically important, because they are the key evidence that enables prosecutors to lock the drug smugglers away in prison for a long time. With the current lancha strikes, there typically is no evidence of what was onboard because in virtually every instance the entire boat, all its cargo, and most or all of its crew or passengers are blown to pieces in the water. We are told by DOD officials that there were illicit narcotics onboard, but little if any real evidence is offered to the public. We are expected to take the government at its word. Where & When Are We Conducting Drug Interdiction Operations? Again, owing to the traditional conception of narcotics interdiction viewed through a law enforcement lens, the Coast Guard typically (though not always) waits until a given drug smuggling vessel is in U.S. waters, because when it is in our waters, and particularly in our territorial sea or contiguous zone, not only are the Coast Guard’s law enforcement authorities at their zenith, but the vessel’s presence there is grounds for a reasonable suspicion that it is bound for the United States with whatever it has onboard. This is not to say that suspicion of a crime is necessary for an at-sea boarding—since 1790 the Coast Guard and its predecessors the Revenue Marine and Revenue Cutter Service have had the lawful authority to conduct suspicionless vessel boardings at-sea (see 14 U.S.C. § 522(a) and 19 U.S.C. § 1581(a)), and the courts have consistently upheld it as non-violative of our 4th Amendment right against unreasonable searches and seizures. The DOD lancha strikes since early September, 2025, have occurred largely in international waters of the Pacific and the Caribbean and, in a few instances, in the waters of other countries. Other than unsubstantiated claims by DOD officials that the boats are bound for the United States, there typically is no indication where they actually are headed. As a general matter, blowing up vessels transiting on the high seas raises serious concerns about violations by the United States of well-settled customary international law. The high seas are open to all countries and all vessels of those countries, which have a fundamental freedom of navigation under customary international law. Why Shift Emphasis from Coast Guard At-Sea Enforcement to Military Strikes on Lanches? Setting aside the apparent obsession with military lethality by some in the current administration and the penchant of others for inhumane cruelty (seemingly as some sort of deterrent), the only rational explanation for the change in approach to at-sea interdiction is that the new approach is more effective in stemming the tide of dangerous, illegal drugs coursing into the United States. Unfortunately, indications are that is not the case. According to a July 28, 2026, front page news story in the Washington Post, mid-year Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and Pentagon reviews have concluded that the deadly military strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats have not reduced the amount of cocaine entering the United States. DEA analysts reportedly found that the lancha strikes have failed to affect the supply or price of cocaine in the United States and have led traffickers to diversify from lanchas in international waters—using different routes running in other countries waters and different means of transportation entirely, such as aircraft. Meanwhile the Pentagon reportedly has concluded that the lancha strikes have had no impact on the purity of illicit narcotics coming into our country. So all indications are we are not accomplishing the presumed goal of this new approach. In the meantime, on September 24, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security announced that the Coast Guard has exceeded 260,000 lbs. of cocaine seized in the Pacific since the start of its Operation Pacific Viper in August, 2025—an operation that appears to be employing all the traditional law enforcement tools described above. I think we are at a point with the DOD lancha strikes where we should be seriously asking ourselves whether the means justify the ends. Regardless, let us please not forget the way we traditionally have tackled this societal problem of illicit drugs and why—our commitment to the rule of law and equal justice under the law, and the reality that the world watches how the United States tackles difficult problems like this. We should be leading by example.
